Prologue.

The order that has been followed in this history is that, first,
in the first books, treatment was given to the gods, and their feasts, and their sa-
crifices, and their temples, and everything concerning their worship: and
with this, the first five books were written: and of these the last is
the fifth book, which deals with the art of divination, which also
speaks of supernatural matters: all these five books were put
into one volume. The sixth book, which forms a volume by itself, treats
of rhetoric and moral philosophy, which these natives attained,
where many kinds of speeches are given, very elegant
and very moral, and even those that concern the gods and their ceremonies
may be called quite theological: in this same book, there is also treatment of the
esteem in which rhetoricians and orators were held. After this it
deals with natural things: and this in the seventh book: and then of the lord
kings, and governors, and principal persons: and then of the merchants,
who after the lords, captains, and strong men are
the most esteemed in the republic; of these there is treatment in the eighth
book: and after them the craftsmen of feather-work, and of gold, and of precious
stones: of these there is treatment in the ninth book. And the qualities, conditions, and
manners of all the officials and persons are treated in the tenth book,
where also there is treatment of the bodily members, and of the illnesses,
and remedies for them: and also of the differences and diver-
sities, and the different kinds of peoples that inhabit this land, and of their conditions:
these four books make up the third volume, which is this one. And
the fourth volume deals with the lower things, which are animals,
birds, herbs, and trees, which make up the eleventh book. And in the
twelfth book there is treatment of the wars, when this land was conquered,
as a horrible thing, and an enemy of human nature.
All these books make up the fourth and last volume.

Chapter one, on the beginning the merchants had in Mexico and Tlatilulco.

Here follows the manner in which the merchants anciently kept their merchandise: when the merchants began trading in the Tlatilulco of Mexico, there was a lord named Quaquapitzahuac. And the principal great traders were two: one was called Itzcoatzin, and the other Tziuhtecatzin. Their merchandise at that time consisted of parrot feathers — some red ones, called cuetal; others blue ones, called cuitlatextli; and other red ones, like the "guana" kind, called chamolli. These three things were their entire trade.

After the aforementioned lord died, they elected another lord named Tlacateutl. And in his time the principal merchants were two: one named Cozmatzin, and the other Tzompantzin. In the time of these men, they began to buy and sell the feathers called quetzalli, the turquoise stones called xihuitl, and the green stones called chalchihuitl; and also cotton mantas, and three more of...

This is the ninth book, which speaks of the merchants, and of those who deal in goods, and how they began with yellow gold, precious stones, and fine feathers.

First chapter: it tells how the trade of the merchants began, in Mexico and Tlatilulco.

Here is set forth how it came about: concerning the merchant's trade, it began in the time of Quaquapitzahuac; those who began the merchant's trade were two merchant lords: Itzcoatzin and Tziuhtecatzin. Thus they traded: what they sold was the red feathers, and the blue feathers, and the chamolli feathers; these three kinds were what the merchants dealt in. And then a second ruler took office, Tlacateuctli; and in his time there were established as merchant lords these two: Cozmatzin and Tzompantzin. In their time there appeared quetzal feathers, not yet long, as well as zacuan feathers, turquoise, and jade, and soft cotton mantas, and soft breechcloths, which were used as gifts; and also all kinds of cotton mantas, little capes, little breechcloths, and little blouses...

Book Nine

Of the rulers mentioned above, the first one was Quauhpoiacaltzin; the second, Nentlamatitzin; the third, Vetzcatvatzin; the fourth, Çanatzin; the fifth, Vei Ocomatzin. At that time, Avitzotzin was lord in Tenochtitlan. In that time the merchants dared to trade in the provinces of Aiotlan and Anasac. The natives of those provinces brought them there as captives for four years in the town called Quauhtenanco, in which they were surrounded by those of Teguantepec, and those of Poatlan, and those of Xochitlan, and those of Amastlatecatl, and those of Quauhtzotla, and those of Atlan, and those of Omitlan, and those of Mapachtecatl. These two aforementioned towns were great towns; many other smaller towns stood against them and kept them surrounded and fought against them. The merchants defended themselves in the town of Quauhtenanca, which was strong; the merchants themselves captured many of the natives, principal people, and many others who were not principal people, who were not counted. The principal ones who were captured wore their insignia as nobles: some wore as insignia the Quetzalpatzactli, others the Xiuhtotvecoatl, others the Tzitzicancoatl, others the Xiuhchimalli, others the Tzeucxtlaiacapapalotl, others wore as insignia...

[Nahuatl text, parallel account:]
There they were seated on mats, on seats — Quauhpoiacaltzin, Nentlamatitzin, Vetzcatocatzin, Çanatzin, Vei Ocotzin. And in Tenochtitlan ruled Auitzotzin. At that time the merchants went in to trade, [to] Aiotlan, Anacac; there they shut themselves in. Four years they remained shut in at Quauhtenanco; there they made war, there those of Tequantepec, Izoatecatl, Xochtecatl, Amastecatl, Quatzontecatl, Atlomitlan Tlacatl, and Mapachtepeoatl made war against them. These named altepetl were all very great. And they could not be overcome, those whom they fought against; rather they themselves overcame [their enemies] as many as they could; there in Quauhtenanco they remained shut in. And these captives became the property of each merchant individually: they were not simply counted among the common people, nor were they reckoned as owners of turquoise; rather they were counted among those possessing turquoise, those who came wearing as their insignia the Quetzalpatzactli, the Xiuhtotoehoatl, the Tzitzicanehcatl, the Xiuhchimalli, the Teuuitlaiacapapalotl, which they put on...

Tzaucuitla nacaztapuztli [ear ornaments made of gummed cotton] for earrings with pendants that hung down to their shoulders, and they carried as banners quetzal-feather banners, also eagle-feather banners, and likewise bracelets called machoncotl. These, it was recounted, were the prizes taken from the merchants; some captured twenty, others fifteen. After the merchants had fought for the space of four years, they conquered the province of Anahuac, and as all of that province surrendered to them, then the Tlatelolcan merchants who had conquered it gathered together, and the most principal among them took the floor and spoke, saying: "O Mexican merchants, now our lord Huitzilopochtli, the god of war, has performed his office in our favor, in that we have conquered this province; now we may safely return to our own land. It is fitting that no one become arrogant, nor consider himself brave because of the captives we have taken, for what we have done is no more than to have opened the way for our lord god Huitzilopochtli. And then they took counsel together, gathering themselves, and said: "O Mexica, merchants, traveling traders: that which has already been done is because of the ruler, the dread one, Huitzilopochtli; it is through him, truly through him, that we have accomplished it. Let it not be said of our fathers, our rulers, that no one shall be credited, no one shall be named as having done it; all of this was done by our elders. We went forth only to seek land for the ruler, the dread one, Huitzilopochtli. And behold, this is our reward, what we have merited: our breasts, the crowns of our heads, were given over for this purpose, so that we might be shown honor, so that we might be credited in Mexico." Folio 4.

...incense, and other perfumes that are used for burning as incense. They also carried shells, which they use to blow in the temples. They also carried bags full of these perfumes. And the leading men and noblemen wore their jackets [richly adorned], which they used when performing sacrifices in the temples. They went along the road as in a procession, in two files: one of the priests, and the other of the lords. They went to join together with them in the town of Atachinaco. And when they had joined with them, they began to burn incense and other perfumes, showing them great reverence, as was anciently the custom.

And once they had performed all the ceremonies that were anciently used in such receptions, they came in order along the whole road ahead of them, and all the people from the surrounding countryside came out along the road to look upon them in great wonder. And when they had arrived at Mexico, no one went to his own house, but all went straight to the house of the lord Ahuitzotzin. And when they entered the courtyard of the palace, they began to burn many perfumes in the braziers that had been made for that purpose, in honor of the gods, where the lord Ahuitzotzin received them with great honor, and spoke to them in this manner: "Beloved merchants and traders, you are very welcome..."

[Nahuatl column:] ...the lord, and the chief men, the leading men, put on their xicolli jackets, and thus they set out; they went in order, they went arranged in rows. And there they went to meet them at Acachinanco. When they arrived, at once they greeted them with incense, they welcomed them, just as had been done since ancient times. And when this had been accomplished, at once those who had gone before came to meet them; all who had gone out to receive them went in order, everyone wishing to see them. And when they arrived, no one went to his own home; rather, at once they went straight on, they went to the palace of Ahuitzotzin. When they reached the middle of the courtyard, then incense was placed upon the fire, as they went to meet the lord Ahuitzotl. He said to them: "O my elder kinsmen, O merchants, O traveling merchants, you have endured hardship, you have wearied and spent yourselves bringing [your goods] here, to the rulers, to the noblemen, who sit here in order, who are honored, who are revered..."

This done, the lord then ordered many precious gifts to be given as a sign of gratitude for their good deeds. He gave them many cloaks, some called "amanepaniuhqui tempapaloio," others called "tetecomaio," others "tetemalacaio," others called "nochpallaxochio" with eight legs. He also gave them loincloths, some called "nochpalmastlatl" with long ends. He also gave to each one a bundle of cloaks of "tuchpanecaiotl" kind; and to each one he gave a bushel of maize and a bushel of beans, and a certain measure of chia.

The pochteca (merchants) were at the conquest of the town of Ayotlan, where they remained under siege for four years. In the fourth year they won and utterly destroyed [the town]...

[Folio 5]

[Nahuatl text, continuing the same narrative in the native language, recounting that Huitzilopochtli had not made it their duty, yet here they performed it on their own account; it truly was fitting that their goods, their possessions, their heads be rewarded — no one shall take it from them, since it is theirs, their property, which they rightfully deserve. And then they were given cloaks — the "amanepaniuhqui," the "tempapaloio," the cloak called "tetecomaio," and the "temalacaio," and the "nochpallaxochio" with eight borders; and the long-tailed "nochpalmastlatl." These were the signs by which it was known that they had entered Ayotlan. And also they were given cloaks, one bundle each of "tochpanecayotl"; and one basket each of maize, one basket each of beans, and one basket of chia, when it was divided among them. And when the war occurred there in Ayotlan, it was there that the merchants, the traders, were enclosed for four years.]

Folio 6.

[Caption:] ...returned with them.

After this conquest, the road being made safe and free to enter the province of Anahuac, with no one hindering them—neither the Zapotecs nor the people of Anahuac—the quetzal feathers and rich plumes that are used here from that time on were first brought by the merchants of Tlatelolco, and they were the ones who used them; and also the lord of Mexico, Ahuitzotzin. These merchants of Tlatelolco were also called captains, and were disguised soldiers in the guise of merchants, who traveled through various regions bordering on and waging war against provinces and towns. The lord Ahuitzotzin wished to distinguish them with gold lip-plugs, which they alone, as a result of that conquest, were allowed to use and no others, as if they were messengers of the king. And the other ornaments that were mentioned above, only they were to use at the great festivals, as was the custom at such feasts...

[Nahuatl text, parallel account:] Then they carried out their duty, those who governed the Mexica, the merchants and traveling traders; they did not turn back, nor did anything stop them from going to war, for that alone was their task, to go and seize it.

And when all was made known, this land of Anahuac, for it had become enemy territory, the Zapotec land, the land of Anahuac: and the fine quetzal feathers, there in Ayotlan, captives were taken; nothing was there yet in Mexico, until then it appeared; many captives were brought to Tlatelolco, which was then under the rule of Ahuitzotzin. And many of these ruling merchants, the disguised traveling merchants, the night travelers, who entered enemy lands: greatly did he reward them, he had gold labrets placed in their lips as recognition; they, together with their sons, became wealthy as a result. And he gave them fine capes, as was said, along with precious loincloths.

All the precious feathers were well guarded and watched over. They were kept separately, each kind housed in its own room; they gave them to the old women who were in charge of them. There were, in correspondence, the featherworkers of Tenochtitlan and the featherworkers of Tlatelolco. And those who were among them worked only on and made the regalia of Huitzilopochtli — what they called the god's cape, the quetzal-feather cape, the hummingbird-feather cape, the turquoise-bird feather cape, which were painted and finely worked with designs — all the kinds of precious feathers were found there. And they also made, in a separate place, the regalia of Moctezuma: what he gave, what he bestowed as gifts upon the allied rulers of the cities — for this purpose the palace featherworkers were summoned and called together, the attendants of the ruler. And there were still others who were called the storehouse featherworkers, who belonged to each of the storerooms that existed, Moctezuma's storerooms: these made whatever merited gear of Moctezuma he would wear in his meritorious acts, in his dances — when a feast day came, he would display himself, he would dance for pleasure, whatever he desired to dance in — for each occasion he finished one thing, for each occasion he made a different thing.

[This chapter speaks of the] houses of these same craftsmen, since there are such people in all parts of this New Spain, and [describes] how they carry out their trades.

[Nahuatl text, describing the process of preparing and painting cotton/feather work:] Thus it is worked, thus the design is made, and it is well polished so that it becomes smooth: then it is spread out, it is covered, the cotton is dampened, it is laid out to dry, it is sought to be good, clear on its face, polished, without roughness, and also even, not lumpy, not knotted: upon it the cotton is dampened, first it is wetted down, it is well soaked: then upon it [the material] is placed, is spread, the fine cotton down is pressed down: first it is well carded, it is pulled apart, it is drawn out, when it becomes like a cloud, like mist, upon it [the material] is pressed down: and it is laid out in the sun, a little while it dries: when it has dried, again it is wetted down, again it is combed, so that it is polished, so that it is made smooth, the cotton, so that it no longer becomes matted, so that the binding adheres well upon it. And when it has dried, when it has become firm, then it is rolled up: then upon it the painted design is spread out, is laid forth.

[This describes] the pattern, with which the design is painted and drawn; it is placed upon the cotton cloth where the painting is to appear. And when it is finished, everywhere the cotton cloth has been painted, nothing having been forgotten, all the pattern having been laid down: then upon it is pasted a paper, bark paper, with which the painted cotton cloth is reinforced and strengthened all over. And then it is bound with a copper tool: it is carried along, hollowed out there, carved out in the recesses of the painting; a small wooden tool called the wood-cutting tool is used for this task — with it the feathers are broken up, cut into small heads, and trimmed round. And when the paper pattern has everywhere been cut out, just as the painting shows it, then it is spread upon the maguey fiber, and there upon it the maguey is marked, following along where the pattern was cut out. When the maguey has been cut out: then it is covered over, smeared, with which the cotton-cloth backing is strengthened; upon the cotton cloth is placed the black color, the paint, wherever it falls in the sun: afterward upon it the feathers are laid down, which are called the binding feathers, the closing feathers, first in front, laid down evenly in rows.

...it is dyed, it is laid out on a board as a pattern. Then begins the arranging, the preparation of feather-work. First the materials are changed and mixed, the paste is dissolved, it is spread with paste, it is glued with paste; with this same substance the paste is also prepared for the young apprentices, those being trained — it is a marvel how it is pasted. Then the black dye, the black color, is cut and applied; with it darkening is done, blackening is accomplished, and with it the painting is carried out. He who does this is very skilled: first the pieces are glued down, then pressed firm with a bone tool. The black color is made from the feathers of the grackle (tzanatl), or else from the scarlet feathers of the macaw, which are dyed. Then, in order, the dyed feathers are laid down, cut to fit, and all the groundwork (the base layer) is made, whatever kind of feather it may be. Whichever one is begun first — as if it were the model — might be the blue cotinga (xiuhtototl), or else the trogon (tzinitzcan), or the roseate spoonbill (teoquechol), or the troupial (atopal), or the hummingbird (xiuhuitzitzilin), the ordinary hummingbird, the quetzal-hummingbird, or the fire-hummingbird (tlewitzilin). In every place where down feathers stand out, their appearance is as if they were blossoming — they glitter and spread out like flowers opening.
